title: Are You Doing Disadvantage Wrong?
author: Dominic Salles
source: Dominic's School Improvement Newsletter, Substack, July 19, 2026
summary: This article makes the provocative case that most secondary schools have virtually no realistic chance of closing the disadvantaged pupil attainment gap, and that Ofsted's pressure on them to do so is both unrealistic and unfair. Drawing on FFT Datalab's polygenic research, the author shows that the attainment gap between disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged students opens by age three and is driven by early home environments—not genetics alone—meaning secondary intervention arrives decades too late to be transformational. Statistical analysis of 2023/24 national data reveals only 42 out of 3,000-plus secondary schools with large enough disadvantaged cohorts actually achieve near-zero gaps, suggesting these are statistical outliers rather than replicable models. The article advises schools to document PP spending against EEF-endorsed interventions meticulously, focus on disadvantaged pupils' progress scores rather than gap-closing as the primary metric, and challenge Ofsted inspectors strategically. The deeper moral argument is that blaming secondary schools for gaps originating in the first three years of life is both wrong and demoralizing.
points: FFT Datalab research shows that even disadvantaged children with high genetic propensity for learning still score significantly below non-disadvantaged peers with identical genetic profiles by age three—before formal schooling begins.

Only 42 out of 3,000-plus secondary schools with significant disadvantaged cohorts show near-zero attainment gaps in 2023/24 data—making gap closure a statistical exception, not an achievable standard for most schools.

By age 16, disadvantaged pupils with strong genetic potential are 20-30 percentage points less likely to achieve top GCSE grades than high-income peers with identical genetic scores, demonstrating how powerfully early environment outweighs later intervention.

Schools should allocate PP funding exclusively to specific, evidence-backed EEF interventions targeted at disadvantaged students—not whole-school initiatives—and measure actual impact rather than assumed effectiveness.

Ofsted inspectors should be challenged with a direct question about which schools are doing this more successfully—forcing them to justify their expectations against actual national data rather than aspirational targets.
quotes: Putting funding into pupil premium is partly a waste of money. We should invest that in the first 3 years of the child’s life to have a much, much higher impact. By the time students get to secondary school there are 20 holes in the dyke and we have only 10 fingers and thumbs with which to plug them.

A strong genetic propensity for education does not protect a child from the effects of a poor early environment. The gaps in development at age five closely mirror differences in early literacy activities, such as being read to by parents or visiting libraries.

By age sixteen, the impact of childhood experience is even more visible. Disadvantaged pupils with high genetic potential are 20–30 percentage points less likely to achieve top GCSE grades in English and maths than high-income peers with the exact same genetic scores.
The idea that most schools can close these gaps is pie-in-the-sky-gold-plated-bullshit.
Stop focusing on the gap - it will be what it will be. Focus on DA P8 and, for the present, A8. If that is getting better, then your efforts are working.
Lets spend the PP funding on your DA students, not suck it into anything else, or anything whole school.
